item.title: Who is Michele Tafoya? Ex-sideline reporter aims to turn Minnesota red in Senate race.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion’s share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers. Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red. In pursuit of that goal, the GOP has put its hopes in Michele Tafoya , a former sports broadcaster and NFL sideline reporter turned politician who polls suggest has a real chance of winning in a state that has been dominated by Democrats in recent election cycles. Tafoya is running for the seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not pursuing re-election. Instead her opponent will be Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan , a progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Minnesota has been at the center of some of the biggest controversies of President Trump’s second term, particularly his administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown. Though a majority of Minnesotans disapprove of Trump’s performance as president, Tafoya has steadily chipped away at Flanagan's lead in polls since the primary. Here’s what you need to know about who she is, what she stands for and how she went from the sidelines to the center of one of the midterms’ most pivotal races. Who is Michele Tafoya? Tafoya was born and raised in Southern California. Her father was an aeronautical engineer, and her mother was a school teacher. She has Hispanic heritage on her father’s side. She married her husband, Mark Vandersall, in 2000. They have two children. Tafoya has been open about her struggles with infertility , which included several miscarriages. Her daughter, Oliva, was adopted from Colombia as a nod to her father’s lineage. After launching her sports broadcasting career in Los Angeles, she moved to Minnesota in the early 1990s to take a job at the KFAN sports radio station in Minneapolis. Before long, she moved on to a national role with CBS, which proved to be the jumping-off point for a decades-long career that made her one of the country’s most recognizable sports broadcasters. She covered five Super Bowls, the NBA and the Olympics — winning five Emmys for her work along the way. Michele Tafoya looks on during Super Bowl LVI, the final game of her storied broadcasting career. Kevin C. Cox via Getty Images Tafoya’s last broadcast was during Super Bowl LVI in 2022. Her political career began the very next day. Less than 12 hours after the game ended, she announced that she would co-chair the campaign of Republican Kendall Qualls in his bid to become Minnesota governor. How did she go from NFL sidelines to the campaign trail? Tafoya has said she always had strong political views, but made a specific effort to keep them out of her work as a broadcaster. “I was not as free to be as vocal about world events that I’m concerned about,” she told The Athletic in 2022. “It’s not because I was told to shut up. I want to be very clear about that. But look, if you’re on a show like Sunday Night Football … the last thing they want to do is invite controversy.” Tafoya was more open about her beliefs outside on social media, where she would regularly promote work from conservative outlets . But she also made statements that broke from the GOP mainstream, including support for efforts to curb climate change. In an interview with Sports Illustrated in 2015, she described herself as a “pro-choice” conservative with “definite libertarian strains.” After retiring from broadcasting, Tafoya made several appearances as a speaker at Republican political events, including the Conservative Political Action Conference. She was also a guest host on The View , taking on the role of the conservative-leaning voice in contrast to the show’s more liberal regular panelists. In 2022, Tafoya launched a podcast that frequently touched on political topics and featured Republican politicians as guests. The most recent episode , released in January, includes an interview with former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell, who unsuccessfully ran for Minnesota governor this year despite an endorsement from President Trump. Tafoya formally announced her Senate bid a few weeks later. In August, she comfortably won a crowded Republican primary to set up a head-to-head race against Flanagan in November. What does she stand for? In her pitch to Minnesota voters, Tafoya has leaned into her sports background. “I’m not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer,” she said while standing on a snow-covered football field in her campaign announcement video. For years, I walked the sidelines when the stakes were the highest, and that job taught me how leadership really works. I’m running for U.S. Senate to bring that experience to Washington and deliver the real results Minnesota deserves. https://t.co/vDbHWpAXg9 — Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) January 21, 2026 Like other swing-state Republicans across the country, Tafoya has worked to find a balance between supporting Trump and pushing back on some of his most unpopular policies. She has supported the president throughout the war with Iran, at one point telling Minnesotans to “take one less trip to Starbucks” to help offset the rising cost of gas. More recently, though, she has joined a growing list of GOP candidates who have called for Trump to end the conflict. “No president of either party should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people. That includes President Donald Trump,” Tafoya told Twin Cities local news KSTP on Saturday. Tafoya added that she would be “inclined to vote to end this war” if given the opportunity in the Senate. She has also said she didn’t agree with ICE’s tactics in Minneapolis and described Trump’s tariff policies as “hit or miss." Her policy views mostly align with mainstream Republican positions. She backs strong immigration enforcement and Trump’s mass deportation campaign, a “tough on crime” approach to public safety, tax cuts, and laws barring transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports. On abortion, she says she agrees with the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade , but personally believes there should be “reasonable access” in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Tafoya’s own opinions of Trump have evolved as well. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Trump not to run for a second term, describing his previous time in the White House as "absolute mayhem.” She also said on her podcast around the same time that there was much about Trump that she found “difficult to accept.” But during the 2024 presidential campaign, Tafoya said she was supporting Trump with “more enthusiasm” than before. She also said she felt “sort of agnostic” on the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. She celebrated Trump’s victory later that year, describing it as “morning in America” — a reference to Ronald Reagan’s famous phrase from the 1980s. Tafoya has mostly left Trump out of her current campaign ads and speeches, instead focusing her messaging on issues like fraud, affordability and public safety. The president opted not to endorse a candidate in Minnesota’s Republican primary and has yet to throw his support behind Tafoya in the general election. What are her chances? Tafoya is one of the few Republicans in major races across the country who is outperforming expectations in the polls. In August, Flanagan held an average lead of about seven points, but Tafoya has been closing the gap . More recent surveys suggest the race is essentially up for grabs. Still, a win by Tafoya would likely be considered a significant upset. Two of the most respected non-partisan elections forecasters — The Cook Political Report and The Center for Politics — list Minnesota’s Senate race as a “likely” win for Democrats. item.title: Guns, voting, immigration and more: The biggest cases for Supreme Court in new term
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Supreme Court began its latest term on Monday with a docket full of high-stakes cases that touch on some of the most contentious issues in American politics, including guns, voting and transgender rights. This will be the second full term for the nation's highest court since President Trump returned to the White House. The previous term, which wrapped up in June, was packed with landmark rulings in a long list of major cases , including Trump's tariffs, birthright citizenship and a slate of key immigration decisions. The justices will likely take on additional cases over the course of the term, but there are already plenty of pivotal cases for the court to consider in the coming months. Here's a rundown of the big cases headed to the Supreme Court this term and what their eventual rulings might mean for the country. Guns Over the past two decades, the Supreme Court has issued a series of decisions that have significantly expanded gun rights. It could go even further next term when it considers whether laws banning certain semiautomatic rifles , like the AR-15, violate the Second Amendment. This category of guns was banned nationwide for a decade until Congress allowed the law to expire in 2004. Similar bans are currently in place in about a dozen states. Gun rights groups have challenged those laws , arguing that it's unconstitutional for these specific types of firearms to be singled out for bans that don't apply to other guns under the Second Amendment. Citizen voting A dozen states currently require voters to show proof of citizenship — like a birth certificate or passport — when they register to vote. The Supreme Court will consider the legality of these requirements again, this time in a challenge to Arizona's latest proof-of-citizenship law in the case Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota . The law is currently blocked by a federal circuit court ruling that called some of its provisions "unlawful measures of voter suppression." Republicans have asked the court to overturn that decision and allow the requirements in Arizona and elsewhere to remain in place. The court's final ruling could have massive implications for voting across the United States. Non-citizen voting is extraordinarily rare and there are already legal measures in place in every state to ensure that only ballots from citizens are counted. That hasn't stopped Republicans from pushing for new laws requiring voters to prove their citizenship. Ballot measures aimed at curbing noncitizen voting will be considered by voters in six states in November. Trump's signature elections bill, the SAVE America Act, would apply the requirements nationwide. Some researchers argue that, rather than preventing fraud, these laws create hurdles that prevent eligible voters from casting their ballots. According to one estimate, as many as 21 million people across the United States lack the documents they would need to be able to vote under proof-of-citizenship requirements. Transgender rights One of the many points of debate around transgender rights in recent years has been the extent of parents' authority over decisions involving their trans-identifying children. The court will weigh in on this issue once again this term when it hears a case challenging a Washington law that gives the operators of emergency shelters the option not to contact parents of runaway transgender youth who are seeking gender-affirming care. A group of parents has sued, arguing that the law violates their parental rights "to raise their child in accordance with the child's biological sex." The pending case runs along similar lines to one decided earlier this year, in which the justices ruled in favor of parents seeking to block a California law that limited when schools can "out" transgender students to their families. Schools In 2020, Colorado voters approved a ballot measure to establish universal preschool throughout the state. As part of the program, state funding is only available to private preschools that meet certain "equal opportunity" standards — including a willingness to enroll LGBTQ students. Two Catholic preschools sued the state , arguing that they were being discriminated against on the basis of their religion by being denied state funding for standing by their beliefs. The state contends that there is no discrimination present because its rules apply to all schools, whether they're religiously affiliated or not. In two similar cases over the past decade, the court has come down on the side of the schools, ruling that states generally can't exclude religious schools from public programs simply because they are religious. Immigration After siding with Trump in a series of immigration-related rulings during its most recent term, the court has agreed to take on three more cases that touch on the heart of the president's immigration agenda. The headline case, which the court agreed to hear just a few days before the start of the term, centers around the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for undocumented immigrants. Historically, migrants who are being considered for removal have had the opportunity to apply for release from detention while they wait for their case to be decided by the courts. Trump changed that policy, causing tens of thousands of immigrants to remain in detention while they await potential deportation. Lower courts have split on the question of whether it's legal for the administration to uniformly deny detained migrants the right to a bond hearing. Now, the Supreme Court will have the final say. A second case centers around Trump's migrant detention policies for a different group of immigrants. The central question is whether migrants with a criminal history, including those who were in the country legally, can be held in detention centers indefinitely, or if they have the right to challenge their detention in court. The case involves two lawful permanent residents who were detained for what they argue was an "unreasonably prolonged" period without a bond hearing. Immigration detention has become a major source of debate during Trump's second term, amid reports of unsafe conditions at detention centers and a striking increase in the number of deaths among detainees. The third immigration case involves immigrants who had once been granted asylum in the United States, had that status revoked and now argue that they should be eligible to become lawful permanent residents. The government argues, and lower courts have agreed so far, that only immigrants with active asylum protection can apply for a green card. Climate change Over the past few years, the Supreme Court has significantly narrowed the government's power to regulate greenhouse emissions in a series of landmark rulings. Next term, it will take up another case that could close off yet another pathway that municipalities have used to try to fight climate change. Lawmakers in Boulder, Colo., have sued oil and gas companies for their role in perpetuating climate change. Those companies have asked the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit. They contend, and the Trump administration agrees , that only the federal government has the power to seek these types of damages because the impacts of climate change go far beyond Boulder's jurisdiction. Several other cities and some states have filed similar suits against the fossil fuel industry. The court could invalidate all of them if it rules in the companies' favor. Jury trials The court will decide whether juries in criminal trials must have 12 jurors . That's already the law in most of the country, but a half-dozen states allow for as few as six jurors in certain cases. The case centers around Hamed Kian, a Florida chiropractor who was convicted of practicing after his license had been suspended following allegations of inappropriate contact with patients. Kian's attorneys argue that the small jury violated his constitutional right to a fair and speedy trial. item.title: Trump says he'll start paying for ads after bipartisan pushback over taxpayer funding
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump said Monday he will start paying for the pro-Trump ads that have blanketed the airwaves in recent weeks with money raised by his super PAC, after his administration drew intense pushback for using public funds on the ads. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," the president wrote on Truth Social . "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc." Emblazoned with the message "Paid for by the U.S. Government," the ads began popping up late last month on national cable and broadcast networks, including CBS, as the November midterm elections approach. Several variations have aired, including one that features a recording of Mr. Trump saying, "We will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America," as photos of the president flash across the screen. Another recounts the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro . CBS News reported last month that there are multiple versions of the ads. The U.S. government produced the content and paid for the airtime through an ad agency. The Department of Homeland Security awarded LMD Agency $20 million for a "National Media Campaign" starting on Sept. 20, contracting records show. A day earlier, the White House Office of Management and Budget granted DHS's Customs and Border Protection $20 million for "OBBB Commemorative Events," according to a nongovernment database. The source of the funds was first reported by The Washington Sun. The White House has defended the ads, calling them public service announcements and denying that they constitute campaign advertisements. A White House official said last month the PSAs "are clearly not political," and noted: "The President is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." Asked about the anti-communism ad, a spokesperson for the White House said: "The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country." The advertising campaign has drawn bipartisan criticism. Democrats have argued the ads could violate federal laws that bar the use of government funds for "propaganda" purposes and limit political activity by executive branch employees. "This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," a group of Senate Democrats said in a letter last month. A handful of Republicans have also voiced criticism. "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said on "Face the Nation." By using his own super PAC to pay for the ads, Mr. Trump is tapping a nine-figure war chest that many Republican candidates hope will be spent in battleground states ahead of the midterms — despite a late start in this election cycle. Since last month, the group has reported tens of millions of dollars in spending on the Texas Senate contest, where Trump-allied Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton is in a tight race against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico. The group had more than $400 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Mr. Trump said last month he is "going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try and help us." item.title: Jim Bakker, televangelist who built a massive empire before scandal, dies at 86
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86. Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear. “He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” she said. The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show “The Jim Bakker Show” there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020. But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on “Saturday Night Live.” A theatrical movie on their lives, “The Eyes of Tammy Faye,” was released in September 2021. At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers’ ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina. Bakker got his start as a traveling preacher Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals. They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children’s show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting “The 700 Club,” a Christian talk show. Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. “The PTL Club” — PTL stands for “Praise the Lord” — became its signature show. When it hit its heyday in the 1980s, “The PTL Club” was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers. The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina. The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s abundant makeup. Sex scandal and financial crimes damage his empire In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell. Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s. Things only got worse. In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years. At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, “On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand.” Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison. Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007. Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched “The Jim Bakker Show” on the PTL Satellite Network five years later. In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic. The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020. Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002. ___ Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary. item.title: ‘Ban the frats’: Protests erupt at Cornell over handling of rape allegation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration at Cornell. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations , demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building. Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses. Protesters shouted , “Ban the frats” and held signs saying, “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting , “Kotlikoff, resign!” The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president’s office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported . The messages in red paint read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED”. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over. The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting “the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”. Related: Before Cornell turmoil, successive US administrations seesawed in attitudes towards campus assaults “We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added. The students’ painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday. “We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.” The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.” The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe’s case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim. According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident. A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation. Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”. The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”. Related: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing. One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said : “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?” And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.” Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office’s handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe’s attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident. Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University. Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said. The Associated Press contributed reporting • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/student-protests-erupt-cornell-over-013011295.html

item.title: Fort Hood shooter to face Army firing squad in 1st such execution since 1945
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army officer and psychiatrist who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday. “Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009,” Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell announced . “He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’ during the attack. “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution,” he continued. “Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.” If Hasan’s execution is indeed carried out by a firing squad, it would mark the first such case for the service since Jan. 31, 1945, when Pvt. Eddie D. Slovik was executed by a U.S. Army firing squad in France for desertion during World War II. The last death sentence carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging at the gallows in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill a young girl. Hasan, who was born in northern Virginia, walked into a Fort Hood readiness processing center on Nov. 5, 2009, and opened fire using a semi-automatic handgun. Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier. Former Army Staff Sgt. Patrick Zeigler, a two-time combat veteran, was shot four times in the attack and spent nearly a year recovering in various hospitals. “He looked me straight in the eyes as he pointed the gun at me, and a split second later, I’m on the floor with a hole in my head,” he told the Killeen Daily Herald in 2023. At his court-martial, Hasan, now 56, admitted to the shooting, and in 2013 said he carried out the attack in support of the Taliban. At the time, Hasan requested a delay in court proceedings so he could ready a new legal strategy that would show he acted “in defense of others.” Asked by presiding Judge Col. Tara Osborn who he was defending, Hasan replied , “The leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban.” Hasan was convicted by a military jury in August 2013, which recommended he be sentenced to death. He was subsequently transferred to Fort Leavenworth, where he has been incarcerated on death row. Jonathan Lehrfeld contributed to this report. item.title: Sen. Tillis calls deciding vote for Hegseth the 'biggest regret' of his career
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth’s turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations. “I know for a fact that there are others like me,” Tillis writes, “Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far.” He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have “expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president’s actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they’d have nothing but nice things to say.” Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a “breaking point” with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically. Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, “my beef is not with him, but the idiots he’s got working for him.” He calls the president “an amazing political talent.” At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to “wake up” and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, “comes back to bite the majority party in the ass.” Tillis also predicts a “bloodbath” for Republicans in November’s midterm elections . “All along, we’ve had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down,” he writes. Regrets his votes for Hegseth and Kennedy The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump’s tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to “intentionally sow disorder” and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets “Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way.” Tillis pushed Hegseth’s confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn’t corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie. On his vote for Kennedy , Tillis writes that “I guess it’s easy to say now, but I’m the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy’s tenure has caused the country as a result.” On both votes, he says he didn’t want to be the deciding factor. “I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward,” he writes. If you oppose Trump on everything, “you lose all influence,” Tillis says. “If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape.” He strongly criticizes several of Trump’s other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Tillis describes his 'breaking point' over the tax bill Tillis’s surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn’t be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his “ Big Beautiful Bill ” of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn’t support the bill’s cuts to Medicaid . Tillis says he thought to himself, “I’m done.” “Everyone reaches a breaking point,” he writes. He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied “I am! DJT.” In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a “QUITTER!” on social media, among other insults. Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response. “I care if you fail and right now we are failing,” Tillis wrote to Trump. item.title: Anger in Japan grows after U.S. Marine is arrested over the killing of a woman
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
TOKYO (AP) — The arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island as Japan’s leaders condemned the crime. The killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to strengthen Japanese military on the island and to work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China in the region. Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island’s capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media. Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone. Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported. “I’m outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder,” Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times. There is longstanding anger over the behavior of some Americans People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, but some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China. Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America’s military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today. There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police. After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime. About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, condemning the crime and renewing demands that U.S. military bases be removed from the island. One sign read: “We’ve had enough of this!” Japanese officials condemn the crime “The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.” Koja said the case underscored the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes. “I’m enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident,” Koja told Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General in Naha, Andrew Ou on Monday when he summoned them to the prefectural government. He demanded that U.S. officials take effective preventive measures. Watson replied: “I recognize the serious incident caused significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbors” and that “we are committed to being good neighbors … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.” In Tokyo, Takaichi condemned the crime and demanded full cooperation and tougher disciplinary and preventive measures by the United States. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also summoned U.S. Forces Japan Commander Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost to his ministry, while Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi expressed his outrage to the U.S. ambassador to Japan, George Glass. The suspect will face Japanese justice Glass, on X, expressed his condolences Sunday to the victim's family and said the United States is cooperating with Japanese authorities. On Monday, he said he is telling U.S. military commanders of the need “to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity" and that he and Watson discussed the “next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities.” Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base. Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks. If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty. item.title: U.S. soldiers wounded in Iranian drone strike say military medical system failed them
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The shrapnel hit Army Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón's body like shattered glass. One chunk of metal lodged into the left side of his jaw. Another piece sliced through his salivary gland before bouncing off his jaw and piercing the back of his neck, severing an artery and embedding in a vertebra. Lincón was among dozens of U.S. soldiers injured in an Iranian drone strike on March 1 . The attack on the second day of the U.S. war with Iran killed six troops who were providing logistical support of critical supplies at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. Whether the military was properly prepared for treating its wounded has become a sharp point of contention. Soldiers and family members have told The Associated Press of a failure to recognize the seriousness of injuries, a poor plan to get the wounded to hospitals and red tape that has hindered follow-up care. The Pentagon has said that the medical care was appropriate. Nine U.S. service members who were wounded spoke to the AP on the record — rare for troops still in the Army — about what they describe as a medical system that left them in many ways fighting to get treatment on their own. The medical care was just one of the military’s failures stemming from the Port Shuaiba attack that soldiers described to the AP. The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting , saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment. The soldiers’ criticism comes against the backdrop of years of disinvestment and drawdowns in the Middle East by multiple administrations and political leaders who sought to end U.S. involvement in the region. Those choices left the region without any major U.S.-run medical facilities. Lincón's wounds included a damaged left vertebral artery, which supplies blood to the brain, and put him at risk for a stroke. That was not considered by the Army to be serious enough to be admitted to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany, a major U.S. military facility, even though Lincón said a nurse there marveled that he was alive. Instead he was sent to the nearby Army barracks and told to schedule outpatient appointments. “I was just kind of on my own, at least it felt like that,” said Lincón, a veteran of wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Lincón's was not an isolated case. Another soldier who had shrapnel removed from his head, Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, said he waited over four months to receive his MRI results. “I’ve had to build my own case for everything,” Ramsbottom told the AP. “It’s very frustrating.” Soldiers helped save each other after Iranian attack After the deadly drone strike, soldiers, who are equipped with tourniquets and trained in first aid, tended to each other and then searched on Google to race the wounded to the nearest hospital in Kuwait City about 20 minutes away. Some of the most seriously wounded soldiers were medically evacuated from Kuwait within two days. Lincón, who was only about 7 feet (2.1 meters) from the blast, spent a week hospitalized there where he had surgery to remove shrapnel from his jaw. He said medical staff told him he had a traumatic brain injury from the force of the blast that ruptured his eardrum and left him briefly blinded. Chief Warrant Officer 4 Rodney Bearman, who had shrapnel embedded from his face to his legs, and some of the other soldiers who were briefly seen at Kuwaiti medical facilities were sent to the homes of U.S. government employees. Iran had unleashed missiles and drones that made it risky for evacuation flights. Some 10 days after the attack, the soldiers were loaded onto a cargo plane. They sat on the floor with straps, including Bearman, who could barely eat or lie down. When they arrived in Germany, Bearman said they learned they were not documented as wounded in combat and would not be hospitalized at Landstuhl. Instead, they were sent to the barracks, as Lincón had been, and told to get outpatient care. Bearman said they were documented that way due to a coding error. “Never did I think that if I was wounded that these things would happen,” said Bearman, who has served for over three decades, including in Afghanistan. “Some sacred trust that I thought would never be broken was broken.” Lincón says he went days without pain medication. He carried a CD with a copy of medical records from Kuwait that he showed the ER doctor at Landstuhl who expressed concern that he had not been evaluated yet by a trauma team. Pentagon says all wounded troops are evaluated Soldiers may not be aware of initial evaluations, like the Army’s battlefield concussion evaluation , that focus on identifying symptoms such as double vision or repeated vomiting and other observations. Troops with mild TBIs and hit by shrapnel often returned to duty quickly in Iraq and Afghanistan. Many soldiers who spoke to the AP did not know the severity of their TBIs. A Pentagon official told the AP that Landstuhl’s mission, especially in battlefield casualty situations, is focused on stabilizing patients to transfer them for more specialized care at a military hospital in the U.S. rather than admitting them. Meanwhile, large hospitals closer to Kuwait have been shuttered. For example, Air Force Theater Hospital at Joint Base Balad in Iraq was handed over to the Iraqi government in 2011 as part of drawdown efforts. In a statement, the Pentagon said that all wounded troops who arrive at its medical facilities are evaluated and may be admitted based on the severity of the injury according to physicians who follow "healthcare-industry practices.” After about a week in Germany, many of the injured soldiers were sent to Fort Hood in Texas, where they underwent the Army's demobilization process to return deployed troops home. Medical records shared with the AP by Ramsbottom and another officer show they were not diagnosed with TBIs until Fort Hood. The officer, who was blown off his chair, said he did not get care for weeks after that diagnosis and had to identify the specialists he needed, like a neuro-ophthalmologist to diagnose the blurred vision from his TBI rather than counting on the military’s medical system. Maj. Billy Key says he did not get specialized care until mid-April when he was sent to a U.S. soldier recovery unit to be treated for his head injury, hearing loss and the smoke inhalation that damaged his lungs. “It took too long,” he said. Dr. James Kelly, chief medical scientist at the Invisible Wounds Foundation, which is focused on military brain injuries, said it’s still not uncommon for a TBI diagnosis to take longer than it should, which could impact a soldier getting treatment as early as possible for the best outcome. “It’s disappointing but not surprising,” said Kelly, an emeritus professor of neurology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. “In a war scenario, it goes on a fair bit.” An initial thorough check should be done by a medically trained person, not simply another soldier, he said. Kelly said that too often medical records note only a concussion, which is in fact a mild TBI, but can be overlooked. Many soldiers are struggling months after the attack Lincón spent seven weeks getting specialized outpatient care at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland, before being sent home to Kansas. Shrapnel is still in his back because it was too close to his spinal cord to remove without risking being left paralyzed. He struggles with dizziness that disrupts his life, he said. He was awarded the Purple Heart and is back on active duty as an instructor at Fort Leavenworth. But his troubles continued beyond medical care. Lincón, who was born in Texas to Mexican parents, was issued only a temporary one-year passport after his passport was blown up in the attack and he was asked for additional documentation to prove his U.S. citizenship. After the AP reached out to the State Department to inquire about his case, the 1995 West Point graduate said he received a call saying the request for more information was a mistake and he would be receiving a passport that would be good for 10 years. “I’m American enough to have fought in three different wars," Lincón said. He’s also concerned his medical records are incomplete. His claim for Traumatic Injury benefits under the Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance was denied due to not meeting the threshold for hearing loss, though it never addressed his other issues, he said. The program gives cash to service members who suffer severe injuries. The Army's Human Resources Command did not immediately respond to an email from the AP asking for an explanation. “I’m fortunate to survive and that’s how I look at it,” Lincón said. “That’s the only way to look at it at this point.” ____ Watson reported from San Diego, Brook from New Orleans and Toropin from Washington. Associated Press journalist Nicholas Ingram in Ankeny, Iowa, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/soldiers-seriously-wounded-iranian-drone-104826233.html

item.title: A common blood pressure drug shows promise for ADHD, animal studies suggest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Dani Serrano/Moment RF/Getty Images) Experts say we need more options for treating ADHD , and a 2025 study suggests one option might already be stocked at the chemist. Around a quarter of patients with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) find that existing medications for the condition do not improve their symptoms. And for others, the benefits of the stimulants commonly prescribed for ADHD are outweighed by the side effects: raised blood pressure, loss of appetite, headaches, trouble sleeping, and the risk of misuse. In a search for alternative treatments, a team of researchers from institutions across Europe has found a common blood pressure medication could be a good candidate: amlodipine, often sold under the brand name Norvasc. In an initial experiment, seven groups of spontaneously hypertensive rats ( which are sometimes used as a model of ADHD ) were each given a regimen of a different treatment and then faced with a regular test designed to assess their movement and level of spontaneity. The only drug that had a significant effect on rat behavior was amlodipine, administered daily for 30 days. ( CDC ) Having identified this potential candidate, the researchers proceeded to test on zebrafish, which were genetically modified to be more hyperactive and impulsive, behaviors we associate with ADHD in humans. When these fish were given amlodipine, however, their hyperactive traits effectively disappeared. In another set of experiments, researchers gave fish methylphenidate (better known by its brand name Ritalin) to see how it compared to amlodipine in terms of curbing impulsivity. Both medications had similarly significant effects when it came to reining in impulsive behaviors. While these animal studies suggest amlodipine could be worth researching further, we still don't know if it would actually be effective for treating ADHD in humans. Just because it seems to have some relevant effects on rats and genetically modified zebrafish doesn't mean it will work the same in humans with real ADHD. But these animal studies provide evidence for scientists to proceed to human clinical trials . The researchers did analyze existing UK Biobank data from people who happened to be taking amlodipine for hypertension, using genetic scores to estimate each person's ADHD risk. While this part of the study is observational (and therefore cannot show cause and effect), it reveals that people taking amlodipine were less likely to report mood swings or risk-taking, two traits linked to ADHD: another hint that this could be worth researching further. The good thing with amlodipine is that it's already approved for treating high blood pressure. In the US, more than 70 million people are taking this drug regularly, which means scientists are well aware of the risks and benefits. While it's generally considered safe, amlodipine comes with its own set of side effects: it can lead to fatigue, nausea, and gum irritation, to name a few. "Repurposing amlodipine, a well-established blood pressure medication, offers a promising and swift pathway to address ADHD symptoms," says neuroscientist Matthew Parker of the University of Surrey in the UK. "Our research indicates that, due to its existing approval and safety profile, amlodipine could be rapidly redeployed as a treatment option for ADHD, potentially providing relief to patients sooner than developing new medications." The research has been published in Neuropsychopharmacology . ScienceAlert stories are written, fact-checked, and edited by humans, never generated by AI. Don't miss a story, subscribe here.
